title: Checkpoint: Deduction and Induction
objective: After this level you can compare deduction, induction and best-explanation reasoning and say how much certainty each gives.
summary: Peirce's bag of white beans, rearranged three ways: deduction guarantees, induction makes probable, and hypothesis (abduction) makes a fair guess.

cards.headline: A handful of white beans on a table. Where did they come from?
cards.body: In 1878 the philosopher Charles Sanders Peirce imagined a room full of bags of beans. One bag holds only white beans, and a handful of white beans lies on the table. Peirce guessed the handful came from that bag. From one little scene he drew all three kinds of reasoning in this chapter.

cards.headline: One bag of beans, three arguments

items.label: Deduction
points: All beans from this bag are white
These beans are from this bag

items.label: Induction
points: These beans are from this bag
So all beans from this bag are white

items.label: Hypothesis
points: All beans from this bag are white
So these beans are from this bag

cards.headline: How much each one promises
cards.body: Same three sentences, shuffled. Deduction runs from the rule to the result, and true premises guarantee it. Induction runs from cases to the rule, so it's only probable: one black bean would sink it, black-swan style. Hypothesis, which Peirce also called abduction, guesses the story behind what you see. He wrote: "As a general rule, hypothesis is a weak kind of argument."

cards.headline: Chapter 2 complete
learned: How deduction, induction and best-explanation reasoning differ in the certainty each gives.
Why a valid argument can reach a false conclusion, and what it takes for one to be sound.
Which if-then arguments are valid, and how to spot the two backwards ones.
Why no pile of white swans proves a rule, while one black swan can sink it.

questions.prompt: In Peirce's bean example, the argument that concludes all the beans from the bag are white is _____.

options.label: deduction
options.rationale: Deduction starts from that rule; it concludes that these beans are white.

options.label: hypothesis
options.rationale: Hypothesis concludes where these beans came from.

options.label: none of the three
options.rationale: One of them reaches the rule.

questions.explanation: Induction runs from cases (these beans, from this bag, are white) to the general rule.

questions.prompt: Match each of Peirce's kinds of reasoning with how it runs.

pairs.right: From the rule to the result
Guesses the story behind what you see

questions.explanation: Deduction runs from the rule to the result. Induction runs from cases to the rule. Hypothesis guesses the story behind what you see.

questions.prompt: Deduction and Induction checkpoint: guessing the handful came from the white bag is which kind of reasoning?

options.label: Deduction, since the bag is all white
options.rationale: The premises leave other sources possible.

options.label: Induction from many beans
options.rationale: It concludes where these beans came from, not a general rule.

options.label: Affirming the if part
options.rationale: No if-then statement is affirmed here.

questions.explanation: Peirce called it hypothesis, also abduction: Level 19's inference to the best explanation.

questions.prompt: An argument is valid and all its premises are true. What can you say about its conclusion?

options.label: It is probably true
options.rationale: Sound arguments do better than probably.

options.label: It might still be false
options.rationale: Not if it is valid with true premises.

options.label: It still needs a counterexample
options.rationale: A counterexample would show it invalid, and it is valid.

questions.explanation: That makes the argument sound, and a sound argument always has a true conclusion.

questions.prompt: "If it's a black swan, it isn't white. This swan isn't white. So it's a black swan." What's wrong with it?

options.label: It denies the then part
options.rationale: It affirms the then part: this swan is not white.

options.label: Nothing at all: it is valid
options.rationale: The swan could be grey, or any other color.

options.label: It has no conclusion
options.rationale: It concludes that this is a black swan.

questions.explanation: It affirms the consequent: the then part is true, so the if part is assumed. A swan that isn't white need not be black.
